title: Credit Rating
subtitle: How do Moody's, S&P, and Fitch assess default risk?
openingQuestion: What is the interest rate difference between an AAA bond and a BB bond?
openingOptions: BB has to pay a higher rate than AAA - higher default risk → investors demand a higher risk premium
AAA pays a higher rate because of its reputation
BB pays a lower rate because fewer people buy it
explanation: A credit rating is a third party's assessment of an issuer's ability to repay debt on time, split into two broad groups: investment grade and speculative grade. The boundary between the two groups matters more than the gaps between notches within a group, because many funds' charters forbid holding the lower group - so a company pushed across that line loses a large pool of buyers all at once, and the bond price falls further than the actual change in risk would justify.

diagram.label: The rating agency assesses repayment ability
Assigns a grade from AAA down to D
The lower the grade, the higher the yield investors demand
Downgraded: bond price falls and new borrowing costs rise

realWorldExample.description: When agencies like S&P or Moody's downgrade the credit rating of a country or a large company, their future borrowing costs rise immediately - an event closely watched because of its direct impact on the entire economy or industry involved.

quiz.question: What is a Fallen Angel?
options: A bond downgraded from Investment Grade to High-Yield
A government bond issued at a below-market interest rate
A bond that has already defaulted and is being restructured
A high-coupon bond issued by a newly established company
quiz.explanation: A Fallen Angel: was once investment grade, and got downgraded to junk (BB or lower). Many funds have a mandate to hold only IG → forced to sell → price drops sharply even though the business may still be viable. This can be a buying opportunity if the downgrade is overdone.

quiz.question: Why does a bond downgraded from Investment Grade to High-Yield (junk) usually trigger a sharp sell-off, far beyond the newly added actual risk?
options: A credit downgrade has no effect on institutional fund behaviour at all, since ratings are only advisory
Because many funds are only permitted to hold Investment Grade, so they must sell
Because it's purely an emotional reaction with no real basis
Because junk bonds always have zero recovery value in default
quiz.explanation: This is the 'fallen angel' phenomenon - when an Investment Grade bond is downgraded to High-Yield, the mandatory investment rules of many large institutional funds trigger a wave of forced selling, creating downward price pressure far larger than the actual change in risk.

quiz.question: Where does the boundary between Investment Grade and High Yield sit?
options: Between A− and BBB+ by international convention
Between AA− and A+ on Moody's scale
Between BBB− and BB+ on the S&P rating scale
Between B− and CCC+ under regulatory rules
quiz.explanation: BBB− is the lowest grade still within Investment Grade; falling to BB+ crosses into High Yield. This boundary matters because many pension and insurance funds are prohibited from holding bonds below that level.

quiz.question: A company is downgraded from BBB− to BB+. What is the most serious consequence?
options: Regulators suspend the company's ability to raise capital
The company must repay all its debt immediately
The bond gets delisted from the exchange
Many funds are forced to sell even though they don't want to
quiz.explanation: The fallen angel phenomenon: fund charters forbid holding below Investment Grade, so selling is mandatory, not optional. The forced-selling wave pushes the price down further than the real credit risk justifies.

quiz.question: Why were credit rating agencies criticised after the 2008 crisis?
options: Because the issuer pays the very agency that rates it
Because rating agencies weren't allowed access to financial statements
Because rating scales differ between countries, making comparison hard
Because ratings are only updated once per fiscal year, so they lag
quiz.explanation: The issuer-pays model creates a conflict of interest: rating agencies compete for contracts from the very entities they're assessing. Many AAA-rated securitised products defaulted within months.

keyTakeaways: AAA→BBB: Investment Grade; BB and below: High-Yield/Junk
Lower rating → higher interest rate (credit spread)
Fallen Angel: an IG bond downgraded to HY → price drops sharply

practicePrompt.question: A corporate bond is rated BB by S&P. Which group does this rating belong to, and how does that affect the interest rate the company has to pay to raise capital?
options: BB belongs to Investment Grade (safe investment), so the company can raise capital at a rate close to a government bond
AAA→BBB is Investment Grade; BB and below is High-Yield, so it has to pay a higher rate
A BB rating has no real practical meaning for determining a bond's interest rate
BB is the highest possible rating, showing the company has almost no default risk
practicePrompt.explanation: AAA→BBB: Investment Grade; BB and below: High-Yield/Junk. A lower rating (like BB) comes with higher default risk, so the market demands a larger credit spread (the rate difference versus a risk-free bond) to compensate for that risk.

summary.keyIdea: AAA→BBB: Investment Grade; BB and below: High-Yield/Junk
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a definition to recite rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Lower rating → higher interest rate (credit spread)

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Look up the credit rating of a Vietnamese or international corporate bond you've heard of, determine whether it's Investment Grade or High-Yield, and check whether the interest rate it pays matches that rating.
application.secondary: If you can't find a published rating, that itself is a risk signal.

sections.text: Before lending anyone money, you want to know the odds they'll repay it on time. For bonds, that assessment is done professionally by rating agencies like Moody's, S&P, and Fitch, packaged into an easy-to-read letter grade.
The rating scale: from AAA to D

The common S&P/Fitch scale runs from AAA (safest) down to D (already in default): AAA, AA, A, BBB sit within the Investment Grade (IG) group - considered safe enough for pension and insurance funds. From BB downward (BB, B, CCC, CC, C) is High-Yield, also called Junk bonds - much higher default risk, in exchange for a higher yield to compensate. Moody's uses an equivalent scale: Aaa, Aa, A, Baa (Investment Grade) and Ba, B, Caa and below (High-Yield). The lower the rating, the wider the credit spread - the extra rate charged over a government bond of the same term.
Fallen Angel: when a bond 'falls in grade'

A notable phenomenon is the Fallen Angel: a bond once in the Investment Grade group gets downgraded to High-Yield (for example, from BBB to BB). The problem isn't just the added risk - many large institutional funds (pension, insurance) are bound by regulations to hold only Investment Grade bonds. Once downgraded, these funds must sell immediately regardless of price, creating a sell-off that goes far beyond the newly increased real credit risk. For an investor who understands this mechanism, this can sometimes be a buying opportunity if the downgrade is overdone relative to the company's actual financial health.

items: Investment Grade (AAA-BBB): safe, low interest rate, suitable for pension/insurance funds
High-Yield/Junk (BB and below): high risk, high interest rate, highly volatile
A downgrade → bond price falls immediately even if the company hasn't defaulted
The three largest agencies: Moody's, S&P Global Ratings, Fitch Ratings - always check ratings from more than one source
